item.title: Comment on The Borda Count is the Best Method of Voting by Dominik Peters
item.description:
I don't think this post accurately describes the properties of the Borda count. The Borda count is among the *most* manipulable voting rules that one can define -- this was already clear in the 1780s when Borda famously said that his system is "only for honest men". Saari's paper at most shows that Borda is least-manipulable in a class of voting rules that are all very manipulable. In general, pointing to Saari cannot establish that there has been a "swing towards the Borda count". Saari has been advocating for Borda for a very long time, and much of his research is better seen as advocacy.

Maskin's paper is okay as it goes, but note that one can weaken IIA in many many reasonably ways, and different rules satisfy different versions. It certainly isn't sensible to say that Borda "avoids defects such as spoilers", since Borda is super sensitive to adding additional candidates.

Generally, if you want good voting rules based on rankings as input, you probably want to go for Condorcet rules (such as split cycle, Schulze, or ranked pairs, or even simple minimax). They are much less manipulable than Borda, are monotonic and Pareto, and are less susceptible to spoilers.

item.title: Comment on The Borda Count is the Best Method of Voting by Abitoftruth
item.description:
Reply to Juanita del Valle:

Any chance of an example of how it can be manipulated?

I'm the red candidate. I get 20 other parties to run. I tell my supporters to ensure the blue candidate is always last and to rank ALL the other candidates in random order to ensure the point differential is the highest between myself and the opponent. Heck. Get 100 different candidates. Make sure that point spread is really wide.
